issue_paraphrase: On Linux systems where an interface carries a /32 IPv4 address (a single-host network, common on VPNs and cloud hosts), psutil reports the interface's own IP address in the broadcast field of the address tuple returned by the networking-addresses function, instead of returning no broadcast at all. A /32 prefix has no broadcast address by definition, and tooling that derives broadcast addresses or copies subnet configurations from this value gets a nonsense result equal to the host's own address.
fix_summary: broadcast_addr() now returns None when the network prefix equals the maximum prefix length (/32 for IPv4, /128 for IPv6); net_if_addrs() recomputes the broadcast from address+netmask on POSIX AF_INET when a netmask is available and nulls it for host-only prefixes. Upstream also added unit tests test_broadcast_addr / test_broadcast_addr_single_host in tests/test_misc.py.
notes: Pure-Python repro, no root, no network, ~1s. Do NOT build the task around configuring a real /32 address on a live interface: it requires NET_ADMIN and mutating the network namespace (the fix's own changelog story was an Alpine box with eth0 configured /32); the golden test + broadcast_addr() direct call are the faithful, deterministic repro. C extension must be rebuilt after git reset (delete psutil/*.so before pip install -e .).

issue_paraphrase: On arm64 Linux builds with shadow call stacks enabled, the kernel prints one /proc/meminfo field (ShadowCallStack) with a fixed-width 8-digit value and no space between the name and the number. When that field reaches ten digits' worth of memory, psutil's function that reports overall system memory usage aborts with a ValueError ('invalid literal for int() with base 10: b'kB'') instead of returning the memory statistics, so callers cannot read total/free/available memory at all on those systems.
fix_summary: virtual_memory() splits each /proc/meminfo line on the first ':' and takes the first whitespace-separated token of the value part, so fields without a space after the colon parse correctly. Same root cause/fix as the later swap_memory() commit d4672602 (issue #2809); the two commits are separate functions with separate regression tests.
notes: No root, no network. Direct repro uses psutil.PROCFS_PATH to point at a scratch dir holding a crafted meminfo; keep the scratch dir out of the repo tree. Golden test uses the project's mock_open_content helper to fake /proc/meminfo. If the agent keeps the repo checked out as the top-level dir (e.g. /tmp/psutil), scripts placed next to it can shadow the installed package via PEP-420 namespace packaging (dir has no __init__.py): run repro scripts from an unrelated cwd and confirm psutil.__file__ points into the installed package. Full suite note: tests/test_memleaks.py imports psleak (skip or install it if running the whole file).

issue_paraphrase: psutil's process iterator silently omits zombie processes from the list it yields, even though zombies are still present in the OS process table and remain fully queryable through the direct process-handle API. Any code that enumerates processes to monitor, kill, or aggregate them misses these entries, and the iterator's internal cache even forgets them as if they had disappeared, so the omission repeats on every call.
fix_summary: process_iter() adds an explicit `except ZombieProcess:` branch before `except NoSuchProcess:` that yields the process instead of dropping it (ZombieProcess is a subclass of NoSuchProcess, so the generic handler was swallowing it). The `if proc is not None` guard covers the case where add(pid) raises.
notes: No root, no network, ~1s. The subtlety that makes this worth authoring: ZombieProcess subclasses NoSuchProcess, so the naive fix (pattern-matching on the reported symptom by creating a real zombie) does NOT reproduce - a real zombie is yielded in both trees because as_dict() already catches ZombieProcess per attribute. The task must use the golden test/mocked as_dict to observe the fail/pass delta. Full suite note: tests/test_memleaks.py imports psleak (skip or install it if running the whole file).
